analysis.one_liner: Raises the legal bar for police to seize and keep private property without a conviction.
analysis.headline: The bill was sent to the Senate Judiciary Committee and never received a hearing or vote before the Congress ended.
analysis.plain_summary: Under civil forfeiture, police can take cash, cars, and homes from people who are never charged with a crime, and the owner has to sue to get their property back while meeting a low burden of proof. This bill would require clear and convincing evidence, a real link between the property and a crime, lawyers for owners, and a judge's involvement in every forfeiture. It would also stop federal agencies from keeping the money they seize and end the program that shares seizure proceeds with state and local police.
analysis.who_benefits: People whose property is seized — often small business owners, drivers, and families who lose cash, vehicles, or homes without being convicted of anything — and, in some cases, people accused of structuring bank deposits, who would get a court hearing within 14 days and the return of their money if police cannot show probable cause.
analysis.who_benefits_short: Owners of seized cash, cars, and homes

how_it_helps.text: The bill raises the government's burden in civil forfeiture from a preponderance of the evidence to clear and convincing evidence, and requires the government to show the owner used the property to facilitate an offense or knowingly consented to its criminal use.

It guarantees the right to counsel in all civil forfeiture proceedings, including appointed counsel for owners who are financially unable to hire a lawyer or for whom the lawyer would cost more than the property itself.
It ends nonjudicial forfeiture outright: no federal seizing agency could take property without judicial process, and only a United States district court could enter a forfeiture order.

It requires written notice of seizure within seven days, moves forfeiture proceeds to the Treasury's General Fund instead of Department of Justice accounts, and eliminates equitable sharing payments to state and local police.

It adds a knowing-intent requirement to the crime of structuring deposits to avoid bank reporting rules, protecting people whose only 'offense' is banking in small increments, and guarantees a probable cause hearing within 14 days with return of the money otherwise.
Owners who win their property back could recover three times the property's value plus attorney's fees.

analysis.who_pays: Law enforcement agencies — federal, state, and local — would lose the seizure proceeds they now spend on their own operations, and the government would pay damages and attorney fees when it wrongly takes property.
analysis.who_pays_short: Federal, state, and local law enforcement agencies

drawbacks.text: Police and prosecutors argue that civil forfeiture is a key tool for dismantling drug trafficking organizations, and that removing nonjudicial forfeiture and raising the standard of proof would make it harder to separate trafficking networks from their money.

Ending equitable sharing removes a funding stream that supports state and local policing; some analysts warn agencies could instead lean harder on state-level forfeiture, which in many states has weaker protections than this bill would create for federal cases.
Moving forfeiture proceeds into the General Fund means the money is no longer dedicated to law enforcement priorities by statute, shifting spending decisions to the annual appropriations process.

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The core change — making the government prove a real connection between a person's property and a crime before taking it permanently — directly protects people who currently bear the burden of getting their own property back. The main costs fall on law enforcement budgets, which is precisely the profit motive the bill is designed to remove. The strongest objection is that some of the same tools police abuse against innocent owners are also used against traffickers; the bill addresses this by keeping forfeiture available, but only through a judge and with a much higher standard of proof.

outcome.mechanism: It was introduced and referred to the Senate Judiciary Committee, where it sat with no hearing, no markup, and no vote until the Congress ended.

narrative.text: Senator Rand Paul introduced the Fifth Amendment Integrity Restoration Act (FAIR Act) on June 25, 2020, joined by three cosponsors: Senator Angus King (I-ME) and Senators Mike Crapo (R-ID) and Mike Lee (R-UT).
The bill was read twice and referred to the Senate Judiciary Committee the day it was introduced.
No further action — no hearing, no committee vote, no floor action — was taken before the 116th Congress ended on January 3, 2021.

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Law enforcement agencies keep the power to seize property through civil forfeiture and to spend the proceeds, and nothing changed for property owners facing the current low standard of proof.

analysis.who_came_out_ahead_short: Law enforcement agencies that seize and spend property

for.name: Sen. Rand Paul
for.what_they_did: Sponsored the bill and introduced it in the Senate.

against.name: Senate Judiciary Committee (no chair action recorded)
against.role: Committee to which the bill was referred
against.what_they_did: Received the referral on the day of introduction and took no further action — no hearing, no markup, no vote — for the rest of the Congress.

against.name: Police and prosecutors' groups
against.role: State and local law enforcement associations
against.what_they_did: Have publicly opposed civil forfeiture reform bills that end equitable sharing and restrict agencies' ability to retain seized proceeds.

sides.party_line_note: The bill's four sponsors spanned parties — one Republican sponsor, one independent and one additional Republican cosponsor — and it died without any vote that would have revealed a broader partisan split.

industries.industry: Federal, state, and local law enforcement agencies
industries.note: These agencies currently keep most civil forfeiture proceeds for their own budgets, including through equitable sharing with local police. The bill ends that self-funding stream and requires judicial process for every forfeiture, so their financial interest runs directly against the property owners the bill protects.

Forfeiture revenue currently flows into DOJ accounts that fund law enforcement activity; the bill redirects it to the Treasury General Fund, removing the financial incentive agencies have to seize aggressively.
Guaranteed counsel and attorney-fee awards would create paid representation for indigent owners contesting forfeitures — the same protection owners of seized property need.

The new knowing-intent requirement and 14-day probable cause hearing for structuring seizures protect small businesses that bank in small increments to avoid reporting paperwork from having accounts wiped out first and arguing later.
